lead: Internal energy U is the energy stored inside matter: molecular kinetic energy plus potential energy from forces between molecules. Enthalpy H = U + pV adds flow work pV to U. The two terms U and pV always appear together when mass crosses a boundary, so H gets its own name. You meet u in a rigid tank and h in boilers, turbines and heat exchangers. Both are state properties, in kJ or kJ/kg.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.1 for Q − W = ΔU, and Unit 1 for properties, state and closed/open systems.

sections.h3: Internal energy is energy stored inside matter

blocks.text: Internal energy U is the energy stored inside the matter. It is the sum of the kinetic energy of the molecules (translation, rotation, vibration) and the potential energy from the forces between them. It does not include the kinetic energy or potential energy of the whole system moving or falling. The unit is kJ, and the specific internal energy is u = U/m in kJ/kg, where m is mass in kg.

U is a state property: once pressure, temperature and phase are fixed, U is fixed. It is extensive: doubling the mass doubles U. We never know absolute U; thermodynamics uses changes ΔU. For a closed system the first law gives Q − W = ΔU, and in differential form δQ − δW = dU. Here Q is heat added in kJ, W is work done by the system in kJ, and dU is the small change in internal energy.

For an ideal gas the molecules have no intermolecular forces, so u depends on temperature T only. Then ΔU = m c<sub>v</sub> ΔT, where c<sub>v</sub> is the specific heat at constant volume in kJ/kg·K and ΔT is the temperature change in K. For steam and other real substances, u also depends on pressure, so use tables (Unit 5).

blocks.where: m is mass in kg; c<sub>v</sub> is specific heat at constant volume in kJ/kg·K; ΔT is final minus initial temperature in K; ΔU is in kJ. Valid for an ideal gas.

sections.h3: Enthalpy adds flow work to internal energy

blocks.text: Fluid entering a control volume is pushed in by the fluid behind it. That push-in work per kg is pv, where p is absolute pressure in kPa and v is specific volume in m³/kg. The entering kg carries its internal energy u and this flow work pv. Enthalpy bundles them: H = U + pV, h = u + pv. H is in kJ, h in kJ/kg, V is total volume in m³.
H = U + pV,  h = u + pv
blocks.where: H is total enthalpy in kJ; U is total internal energy in kJ; p is absolute pressure in kPa; V is total volume in m³; h and u are specific values in kJ/kg; v is specific volume in m³/kg.

blocks.text: Take changes: ΔH = ΔU + Δ(pV). For an ideal gas pV = mRT, where R is the gas constant in kJ/kg·K and T is absolute temperature in K. Then Δ(pV) = mRΔT. Using ΔU = m cv ΔT gives ΔH = m(cv + R)ΔT = m cp ΔT, where cp is the specific heat at constant pressure. The proof that cp − cv = R is in Chapter 2.3.

At constant pressure in a closed system, with only pV work, the heat added is Q<sub>p</sub> = ΔH. In a steady-flow heat exchanger with no shaft work, q = Δh per kg. During a phase change at constant pressure, the latent heat is an enthalpy change, such as h<sub>fg</sub> for steam (Unit 5).

Enthalpy is not heat. 'Heat content' is a loose name. Heat Q is energy in transit and depends on the path; H is a state property fixed by the state. Q equals ΔH only in the constant-pressure case above. Do not write H = Q.

Read the process before choosing a formula. A closed rigid tank has no boundary movement, so W = 0 and Q = ΔU = m cv ΔT for an ideal gas. A closed piston–cylinder at constant pressure has Q = ΔH = m cp ΔT. A flow device such as a turbine or nozzle uses h in the steady flow energy equation (Chapter 2.6).

For steam, compressed liquids and refrigerants, c<sub>p</sub> is not constant and u, h come from property tables. The bookkeeping still holds: Δh = Δu + Δ(pv), but you read h directly from the table instead of integrating a specific heat. This is why the Mollier chart plots h against s (Unit 5).

figure.caption: Internal energy and flow work add to give enthalpy, the property that appears when mass crosses a boundary.

spec.title: Enthalpy bundles two terms
spec.aria: Internal energy and flow work are added together to give enthalpy.

examples.question: 2 kg of air (R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K, c<sub>v</sub> = 0.718 kJ/kg·K, c<sub>p</sub> = 1.005 kJ/kg·K) is heated at constant pressure from 300 K to 400 K. Find ΔU, ΔH and Δ(pV).
steps: Data: m = 2 kg, R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K, c<sub>v</sub> = 0.718 kJ/kg·K, c<sub>p</sub> = 1.005 kJ/kg·K, T₁ = 300 K, T₂ = 400 K. ΔT = 400 − 300 = 100 K.
Check: ΔU + Δ(pV) = 143.6 + 57.4 = 201.0 kJ, matching ΔH.
examples.answer: ΔU = 143.6 kJ, ΔH = 201.0 kJ and Δ(pV) = 57.4 kJ.
examples.check:
m = 2.0
R = 0.287
cv = 0.718
cp = 1.005
dT = 100.0
dU = m * cv * dT
dH = m * cp * dT
dpV = m * R * dT
print(round(dU, 1))
print(round(dH, 1))
print(round(dpV, 1))

traps: Using ΔH = m c<sub>p</sub> ΔT for a closed rigid tank. A rigid tank has constant volume, no flow work, and Q = ΔU = m c<sub>v</sub> ΔT for an ideal gas.
Adding R to c<sub>v</sub> when R is in J/kg·K and c<sub>v</sub> is in kJ/kg·K. Convert R = 287 J/kg·K to 0.287 kJ/kg·K before adding.
Calling enthalpy 'heat content'. H is a state property; heat Q is a path function. Q = ΔH only at constant pressure with no other work.
Writing ΔH = ΔU + pΔV in every process. The correct form is ΔH = ΔU + Δ(pV); pΔV alone is valid only at constant pressure.
Using c<sub>p</sub> ΔT for steam or refrigerants. For real substances h comes from tables because h depends on both T and p.

quiz.q: Define internal energy U and give its unit.
quiz.a: U is the energy stored inside matter: molecular kinetic energy plus potential energy from intermolecular forces. Unit: kJ; specific internal energy u is in kJ/kg.

quiz.q: Write the defining equations for H and h.
quiz.a: H = U + pV and h = u + pv. H is in kJ, h in kJ/kg, p is absolute pressure, V is total volume, v is specific volume.

quiz.q: Why does enthalpy bundle the pV term with internal energy?
quiz.a: Fluid entering a control volume carries u plus the push-in flow work pv. These two always travel together when mass crosses a boundary, so H = U + pV is a useful single property.

quiz.q: Why is 'heat content' a poor name for enthalpy?
quiz.a: Heat is energy in transit and depends on path; enthalpy is a state property. Q = ΔH only for a constant-pressure process with only pV work.

quiz.q: 1.5 kg of air (c<sub>v</sub> = 0.718, c<sub>p</sub> = 1.005, R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K) is heated at constant pressure through 80 K. Find ΔU, ΔH and Δ(pV).
0.5 kg of air in a rigid tank (c<sub>v</sub> = 0.718, c<sub>p</sub> = 1.005 kJ/kg·K) is heated through 50 K. Find Q and ΔH.
quiz.a: Rigid tank: W = 0, Q = ΔU = 0.5 × 0.718 × 50 = 17.95 kJ. ΔH = 0.5 × 1.005 × 50 = 25.125 kJ. Q is not equal to ΔH here.

quiz.q: A student uses Δh = c<sub>p</sub> ΔT for steam in a boiler. What is wrong?
quiz.a: Steam is not an ideal gas; c<sub>p</sub> is not constant and h depends on pressure and temperature. Use steam tables: Δh = h₂ − h₁.

quiz.q: For an ideal gas, why do u and h depend only on temperature?
quiz.a: An ideal gas has no intermolecular forces, so molecular potential energy is fixed. Internal energy is only molecular kinetic energy, set by T. Since pV = mRT, h = u + pv is also a function of T only.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, enthalpy is the working property for boilers, condensers, evaporators and heat exchangers; steam tables and the Mollier chart list h directly. Chemical engineers use standard enthalpy of formation for reactor energy balances. HVAC engineers use moist-air enthalpy in psychrometry.
